title: High blood pressure among children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus in Uganda: A multicenter cross-sectional study
content:
by Charles Mwendwa Mutisya, Martin Nduwimana, Dickson Kajoba, Grace Ndeezi

Background

The coexistence of diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (HTN) worsens the clinical outcomes of children with diabetes concerning both microvascular and macrovascular disease. It increases mortality risk by 5 times, with a higher risk of death in developing countries. Therefore, comprehensive care for patients with diabetes, including hypertension screening, must be provided.

Methods

This multicenter health facility-based cross-sectional study included 150 children and adolescents aged from 6 months to 18 years with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) who were treated at Jinja Regional Referral Hospital (JRRH), Mbale Regional Referral Hospital (MRRH) and Lira Regional Referral Hospital (LRRH). Interviewer-administered questionnaires were used to obtain data, which were then analyzed according to the study objectives using STATA® version 18. High blood pressure diagnosis was based on blood pressure (BP) above or equal to the 90th percentile for <13 years and either systolic BP ≥ 120 mmHg or Diastolic BP ≥ 80mmhg for 13 years and older for age, sex and height. The prevalence of high BP was determined as a percentage, whereas associated factors were analyzed at both bivariate and multivariable logistic regression. The significance of associations was set at a p-value <0.05 and a 95% confidence interval.

Results

Of the 150 participants, 115 (76.7%) were above 12 years of age, and the median age was 15 years (IQR 13–17). There were more females [81/150 (54%)] than males. The majority were attending school [130/150 (86.7%)], with a few attending boarding school [26/130 (20%)]. Sixty-one participants (40.7%, 95% C.I 33%−49%) had high BP, and 53 (86.9%) of these patients had poor glycemic control. The factors associated with high BP among T1DM participants included having diabetes for 4–8 years (aOR= 2.23 [95% CI: 1.05–4.75]; p = 0.037), and 9–12 years (aOR= 4.545 [95% CI: 1.075–19.221]; p = 0.040) respectively compared to those less than 4 years. Additionally, having Poor glycemic control (HBA1C ≥ 7%) increased odds for high BP by 2.905 [95% CI: 1.149–7.342]; p = 0.024) times compared to their counterparts with good glycemic control.

Conclusion

There was a high prevalence of high blood pressure among children with type 1 diabetes. Factors associated with high blood pressure included disease duration of more than 4 years and poor glycemic control.
